turns.prompt: A least-recently-used (LRU) cache with a fixed capacity is often built from a hash map plus a doubly linked list of entries ordered by last use. What does each part contribute? turns.answer: The hash map gives us direct O(1) average lookup from a key to its node in the doubly‑linked list, while the list maintains the entries in recency order so the most‑recent item is at the head and the least‑recent at the tail. On a cache hit for key k, the map yields the node, we splice it out by rewiring its prev/next pointers and then insert it at the head, updating the head pointer; this costs only a constant number of pointer and map operations. A put works similarly: if k already exists we update its value and move its node to the head; if it’s new we create a node, add it to the head and to the map, and when the capacity is exceeded we remove the tail node and delete its key from the map. Because each operation involves only a fixed‑size hash lookup and a few pointer changes, both get and put run in O(1) average time.
